home.title: CUZDEV — Made with AI. Made to play.
home.meta: Explore ZZZombie Assault and Floki Heaven: independent games in development, with real screenshots, original sprites and detailed game pages.

play.
home.description: Big worlds. Small-team energy. We use AI to build the games we want to get lost in, then test, tweak and keep playing.
home.games_intro: A zombie outbreak on the ground. A rabbit adventure in the sky. Get to know the worlds, combat and systems already in each game.
home.z_hook: The world ended. Your story didn't.
home.z_body: An open-world action adventure with spell-and-sword combat, abandoned towns, a frozen north, desert roads and a neon city. Recruit allies, build your hero and explore with a local co-op partner.
home.f_body: A rabbit with an arsenal, floating islands and far too many bullets. Jump through danger, combine upgrades and cross seven procedural floors in a shooter roguelite built around the next run.
home.about_lead: We use new tools to make games we want to play.
about_body: AI helps with code, procedural art, experiments and tests. The screenshots here come from the games themselves, and the animated characters use their original sprites.
We still have to check the result: does the combat work, can you read the scene, and is there a reason to keep exploring? We test and revise before keeping a change.
home.about_note: AI-assisted development describes our production workflow. It is not a promise of generative AI running inside the games.

zzz.meta: Discover ZZZombie Assault: an open world, Akashi and Satoshi, elemental combat, skill trees, equipment, living shelters, optional survival and local co-op.
zzz.intro: Wake up in the ruined Hélix laboratory and find your way through a world that keeps moving without you. Magic, steel and scavenged equipment help you face the outbreak; the road decides what you find next.
akashi: Akashi fights with magic at range and a blade up close. Fire, water and void spells share his skill tree, while sword hits and parries help restore mana. His coat and hair use the original wind-animated frames shown here.
Akashi standing with his coat moving in the wind.
satoshi: Satoshi can chill and freeze enemies, pull them with wind and use light for protection. His default right-click technique is a three-strike sword combo. The animation below plays the original slash1, slash2 and slash3 frames in order.
Satoshi performing his original three-strike right-click sword combo.
zzz.party_intro: Nine allies join the chosen protagonist through the campaign. You can switch heroes and keep building the party; each has its own combat style.

world: Explore the world, not just the next objective.

The mainland connects Ridgewood's streets, small towns, farms and dense woodland with the coast and a large southern desert. Neo-Vale changes the scenery again with industrial districts, neon signs and rain-soaked streets. In the north, taiga and snowfields lead to frozen lakes, glaciers and Aurora Refuge.

The world also has a ring of twelve offshore islands. A monastery, prison, ship graveyard, naval base, laboratory and volcanic crater each give you another reason to leave the mainland. Roads, landmarks, hidden stashes, notes and lookouts reward detours; the map reveals areas as you discover them.
Aurora Refuge at dawn: warm low sunlight and long shadows across the snow.
Neo-Vale's neon streets in the rain.
Desert roads and red terrain beyond the towns.
heroes: Choose Akashi or Satoshi before starting a new game. Both combine ranged spells with close combat, but their elements and techniques lead to different builds. The other protagonist can join as the second player in local co-op.

Rex brings a rifle and explosives; Kenji relies on fast sword attacks; Claire drains life and controls infected servants. Brutus throws enemies, Nina sets up turrets, and Wade fights alongside Sparky. Cole, Tony and Ivy add ricochets, a chainsaw and long-range fire to the party.
The in-game protagonist selection screen: Akashi and Satoshi.
combat: Use magic at range and steel up close.

Mouse attacks are the starting point. Akashi can throw fire, shape water and pull a crowd into a black hole; Satoshi works with ice, wind and light. Their blades consume stamina, while spells spend mana. A melee hit can help pay for the next spell, so switching distance is part of the fight.

Guns, crossbows, punches, traps and turrets give the recruited heroes different roles. Dodges avoid attacks, parries reward timing, and heavy hits shove bodies and loose objects. Fire, freezing, poison and shock can also come from equipment, with visible changes to attacks and enemy deaths.
Akashi using a fire spell in the game.
A void attack pulling enemies toward its center.
skills: Heroes begin with their mouse attacks. Skill points unlock Q, E, R and F, improve attacks and open build paths. The HUD only shows abilities you have unlocked, so a new hero does not start with every skill available.

The protagonists can assign alternative spells to the same button. Akashi's tree supports fire, water, void and blade builds; Satoshi has ice, wind and light options. Other heroes have their own branches and technique variations. You are choosing an attack pattern and resource loop, not just adding damage to every stat.
Akashi's skill tree, with selectable nodes and spell alternatives.
gear: Equipment changes the fight and the silhouette.

Loot fills eight slots: weapon upgrade, head, armor, gloves, boots, backpack, belt and accessory. Compare a new item with the equipped one before replacing it. Higher-rarity pieces can add effects such as burning hits, chain lightning, freezing, piercing shots or a combat drone.

Biome sets reward wearing matching pieces. The Polar set combines cold protection with freezing effects; Kaizen equipment adds drone support. Unique boss drops and hero relics give more specific bonuses. Wearable pieces also appear on the character, including headgear, coats, boots and backpacks.
The equipment inventory, with slot icons and an item comparison.
The Polar set displayed with its visible aura and equipment effects.
workshop: Shelter workshops turn scavenged scrap into permanent upgrades, supplies and equipment improvements. Reforging gives you a way to work on a promising piece instead of waiting for a replacement. The item panel shows what you are changing before you spend the resource.

Scrap also matters away from the workbench: merchants, medicine and other services compete for the same supply. A good haul can support a new build or prepare you for a longer trip. Boss loot, contracts, stashes and salvage feed that loop.
The workshop's reforging interface, showing an item and the available action.
quests: Follow a story, then take a detour.

The main questline connects the outbreak, towns, rescued heroes and Hélix. Most regional missions can start when you reach their location rather than forcing you through every earlier task. After a detour, the tracker can return you to the main story.

Shelter jobs, contracts and parallel sagas add rescues, supply recovery, named elites, nests and local stories. Defense and area-clearing objectives use enemy waves; escorts and generator objectives give those fights a purpose. Conversations and the journal let you track what you accepted instead of relying only on a waypoint.
The contracts screen with available tasks and rewards.
A resident conversation that offers a regional story.
shelters: People still live behind the walls.

Shelters are safe places with different layouts, residents and services. Hopewell has its own village life; Port Haven opens toward the sea; Aurora Refuge sits in the snow. Mechanics, merchants, doctors and notice boards support the trips between them.

Caravans, scavengers and patrols travel the roads and can need help. The honor system records how you treat them: rescuing people or robbing travelers changes prices, help from patrols and how shelters or raiders respond. Camps outside the walls can come under attack, so an encounter can leave a consequence in the world.
threat: A crowd is not the same as a boss.

Runners close distance, spitters pressure you from range, shields punish frontal attacks and screamers draw more infected into a fight. Regional enemies change the mix again. Elites carry stronger threats and better loot; bosses mark major attacks before committing to them.

World events interrupt the route with danger or a reward. Fighting builds threat and can trigger a Fury Wave. Blood-moon encounters, nests, ambushes and guarded treasure keep exploration from becoming an empty walk between quest markers.
A blood-moon development capture with the Fury Wave interface.
weather: Watch the light change over the snow.

The game moves through blue predawn light, warm sunrise, bright midday and evening color. The sun and moon change the direction and length of shadows. Lamps, fire, spells and city signs give their own light to a night scene.

Weather changes gradually. Rain, fog, wind and storms alter the atmosphere and visibility; northern snow and desert sandstorms belong to their regions. The dawn refuge image here is captured from the game itself, with its original lighting and shadows, rather than painted for the website.
Morning light and directional shadows at Aurora Refuge.
Rain and glowing signs in Neo-Vale after dark.
travel: A horse helps off the road, while a motorcycle favors asphalt and struggles in difficult terrain. Docks connect the mainland and offshore islands by ferry. Once you have reached a dock, it becomes part of the network you can revisit.

You can also swim in deep water, dive with an oxygen supply and look for submerged chests. An inflatable motorboat makes longer water trips faster, but keeps your hands away from attacking. Islands add their own terrain, enemies, bosses and unique loot rather than functioning as a single final destination.
The mainland dock facing Lighthouse Island.
survival: Survival is a choice, not a forced rule.

The optional Survival Mode is selected when starting a new game and stays with that save. It adds fatigue and cold, makes night and exposure more costly, and restricts saving to shelters. The normal campaign remains available without those rules.

Resting, warmth and shelter planning matter more in this mode. A route through the frozen north needs a place to recover, and a trip after dark needs a reason to risk it. The extra HUD meters show the condition you are managing instead of hiding the penalties.
The Survival Mode HUD displaying fatigue and cold at night.
The shelter rest menu for recovering before another trip.
coop: Share a screen, then split the view.

Two people can play on the same computer. Player one uses keyboard and mouse; player two can use a controller or the supported second keyboard controls. The shared camera pulls back while you stay together and switches to a vertical split when you move too far apart.

Each player has a backpack, equipment and skill choices, while party level and scrap are shared. A fallen player waits for the partner to revive them; if both fall, the group returns to safety. Local co-op is in the current build. Online co-op is not available yet.
Two local players together in the shared camera view.
The vertical split-screen view when the players separate.

zzz.end_body: This page describes systems in the current development build. We are still revising the combat, world and presentation. A public release date and a download are not announced here.

floki.meta: Explore Floki Heaven: a rabbit shooter roguelite with seven procedural biomes, twelve weapons, item combos, active equipment, travelers and three current boss types.
floki.intro: Floki is a small rabbit crossing floating islands with an unreasonable amount of firepower. Shoot, jump and choose your upgrades as a procedural route carries you through seven floors.
sprite: The game keeps its pixel-art rabbit and adds visible upgrade combinations as the run develops.

combat: Floki aims with the mouse and fires with the left button. The jump lifts him above incoming bullets, with a ground shadow that helps you read where he will land. A blank clears hostile bullets and pushes enemies away when the screen gets crowded.

Hits have knockback, and enemies can collide, bounce against obstacles or fall from an island when pushed out. Recoil, impact pauses, muzzle flashes and damage feedback make different weapons feel different. Jumping still requires watching the landing area; it does not clear the whole room for you.
A normal combat capture with Floki shooting on a floating island.
world: Seven biomes, a different route each run.

The current run crosses Sky Islands, Autumn Grove, Twilight, Storm Ruins, Frost Garden, Spore Refuge and Ash Crown in a shuffled order. A seed builds the room network, bridges, encounters, props and rewards rather than replaying one fixed route.

Larger floors have optional branches with useful exploration events. Combat rooms close their gates until you clear them, while treasure, shopping, activities and the boss provide reasons to choose a path or come back. Hidden caches reward looking beyond the direct route.
A hidden cache on an optional exploration route.
An icy island in the development build.
An ash-colored island with a local activity.
weapons: Build around the weapon you find.

Twelve weapons cover a starting shotgun, revolver, rapid fire, an arcane staff, rockets and a sword, plus unlockable alternatives. Aurora Carbine favors precision; Lead Bloom sends a wide pellet fan; Moon Needle pierces enemies; Prism uses bouncing crystals.

Twenty-three passives and three curses modify the run. Five named combinations add extra effects. Cloud Guardian can clear nearby bullets on landing, Pocket Storm adds fragments to a final ricochet, and Explosive Feast charges healing through kills. Several upgrades also stack visible changes on Floki, such as wings, spikes or a crystal plate.
Floki wearing several original visual upgrade layers.
active: One active slot. Make it count.

Barrier gives brief protection, Decoy distracts ordinary enemies, and Sentry places a short-lived turret with its own shots. You carry one active item at a time and use it with C. A preview shows what you are accepting before you equip it.

Four distinct kills recharge the item; swapping equipment does not provide a free refill. The inventory shows your current active alongside weapons and passives. Turret projectiles respect obstacles, so placement matters as well as timing.
The inventory showing the equipped active item and its charge.
An active Sentry fighting in the game.
exploration: Stop for the people and the side paths.

Íris, Lume and Gomo appear as travelers you can meet during exploration. Conversations, secrets and activities become discoveries in the Journey collection. These encounters are part of the procedural world, not a fixed traveler assigned to each of the first three floors.

A campfire restores health and ammunition for coins. A forge offers a choice of one of three relics, and a challenge crystal starts an optional fight with a reward after you clear it. Completing the activity, rather than only opening its menu, counts toward the related objectives.
A campfire encounter on the expanded map.
A forge offering an optional relic choice.
The challenge crystal and its combat area.
A traveler conversation in the development build.
bosses: Learn the warning before the attack.

Demonic Centipede, Root Guardian and Eclipse Watcher are the three boss types currently implemented. They are shuffled across the seven floors without immediate repeats, with difficulty increasing as you progress. Seven floors does not mean seven unique bosses in this build.

Charges, rings and directional bullet patterns have wind-up cues that give you a chance to reposition. The Guardian and Watcher have their own active and warning poses. Victory follows the boss on the seventh floor; the route before it can vary with each run.
Root Guardian during one of its attack patterns.
Eclipse Watcher during a boss encounter.
journey: Unlock more ways to start again.

The Journey records objectives, arsenal, relics, bestiary, equipment and discoveries across normal runs. Goals unlock additional weapons, relics and starting active choices. You can select an unlocked starting weapon in the Arsenal before the next run.

This progress adds variety rather than permanent purchases of health or damage. Defeating enemies reveals bestiary entries and practical hints; meeting travelers and completing exploration goals opens other starting choices. The collection gives you something to work toward even when a run ends before the last floor.
The Journey collection with starting equipment choices.

floki.end_body: Floki Heaven is still in development. This page covers the systems and content already in the build; future bosses and campaign additions will be shown here when they are implemented. We have not announced a public release date or download.
